# Sirach 51 — Disagreement Log

**Chapter:** Sirach 51 | **Date:** 2026-03-17 | **Total Disagreements:** 21

---

## Disagreement 1 — 51:1, "O Lord, O King" vs. "Lord and King"

**EMET:** "I will give thanks to you, O Lord, O King"
**LOGOS:** "I will give thanks to you, O Lord and King"
**PNEUMA:** "I give you thanks, Lord and King"
**Issue:** Greek Kyrie basileu = O Lord, O King (two vocatives). EMET preserves both vocatives separately; LOGOS joins them; PNEUMA drops the "O."
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "O Lord, O King" — two separate vocatives gives the opening address its solemn force.

---

## Disagreement 2 — 51:2, "protector and helper" vs. "shield and helper"

**EMET:** "you were a protector and helper"
**LOGOS:** "you have been my protector and helper"
**PNEUMA:** "you have been my shield and helper"
**Issue:** Greek antilēmptōr = helper, one who takes hold on behalf of. "Protector" (EMET/LOGOS) is more general; "shield" (PNEUMA) is more vivid but interpretive.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "protector and helper" (EMET/LOGOS).

---

## Disagreement 3 — 51:2, "redeemed my body" vs. "delivered my body"

**EMET:** "redeemed my body from destruction"
**LOGOS:** "delivered my body from destruction"
**PNEUMA:** "saved my body from destruction"
**Issue:** Greek errusō = rescued, saved. "Redeemed" (EMET) has theological overtones of ransom payment; "delivered" (LOGOS) is more neutral; "saved" (PNEUMA) is the most general.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "delivered my body from destruction" — neutral and appropriate.

---

## Disagreement 4 — 51:2, "trap of a slanderous tongue" vs. "snare"

**EMET:** "from the trap of a slanderous tongue"
**LOGOS:** "from the snare of a slanderous tongue"
**PNEUMA:** "from the noose of a slanderous tongue"
**Issue:** Greek pagidon = trap, snare. "Snare" (LOGOS) is the more common biblical word; "trap" (EMET) is equally valid; "noose" (PNEUMA) implies strangulation.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "from the snare of a slanderous tongue" (LOGOS).

---

## Disagreement 5 — 51:3, "grinding teeth about to devour me"

**EMET:** "from grinding teeth about to devour me"
**LOGOS:** "from grinding teeth about to devour me"
**PNEUMA:** "from teeth grinding to devour me"
**Issue:** Greek odontōn syntriphontōn = of grinding teeth. EMET/LOGOS agree. PNEUMA restructures slightly. All convey the same vivid image.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows EMET/LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 6 — 51:4, "choking fire" vs. "smothering fire" vs. "suffocating fire"

**EMET:** "from the choking fire on every side"
**LOGOS:** "from the suffocating fire on every side"
**PNEUMA:** "from smothering fire on every side"
**Issue:** Greek pyros parakaiomenēs = fire burning alongside/enveloping. "Smothering" (PNEUMA) implies extinguishing; "suffocating" (LOGOS) implies the fire consuming air; "choking" (EMET) is apt.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "smothering fire on every side" — "smothering" best captures the enclosing quality of the fire.

---

## Disagreement 7 — 51:5, "belly of Hades" vs. "pit of Hades"

**EMET:** "from the depth of the belly of Hades"
**LOGOS:** "from the deep belly of Hades"
**PNEUMA:** "from the pit of the belly of Hades"
**Issue:** Greek ek gastros hadou = from the belly of Hades. "Belly" (EMET/LOGOS) is most literal and most striking (Jonah 2:2 echo). PNEUMA's "pit" substitutes a different image.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "from the depth of the belly of Hades" — the Jonah echo is significant and the grotesque image is deliberate.

---

## Disagreement 8 — 51:6, "a false tale to the king" — who is the king?

**EMET:** "a false tale to the king by a wicked tongue"
**LOGOS:** "slander delivered to a king by a treacherous tongue"
**PNEUMA:** "lies told about me to the king by a treacherous tongue"
**Issue:** This is autobiographical. Ben Sira describes being slandered before a ruler. PNEUMA adds "about me" for clarity. LOGOS uses "treacherous" for the tongue's quality; EMET uses "wicked."
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "slander delivered to a king by a treacherous tongue" (LOGOS) — "treacherous" is stronger and more specific.

---

## Disagreement 9 — 51:8, "called to mind" vs. "remembered"

**EMET:** "I remembered your mercy, O Lord"
**LOGOS:** "I called to mind your mercy, O Lord"
**PNEUMA:** "I remembered your mercy, Lord"
**Issue:** Greek emnēsthēn = I remembered. EMET/PNEUMA are more literal; LOGOS "called to mind" is slightly more deliberate/active.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "I called to mind your mercy" — the deliberate act of recollection is important in the psalm structure.

---

## Disagreement 10 — 51:9, "lifted up my supplication" vs. "lifted up my prayer"

**EMET:** "I lifted up my supplication from the earth"
**LOGOS:** "I lifted my prayer from the earth"
**PNEUMA:** "I lifted my prayer up from the earth"
**Issue:** Greek proseukhēn = prayer. EMET "supplication" is more specific; "prayer" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) is more general.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "I lifted up my prayer from the earth" (LOGOS) — "prayer" is the standard term for proseukhē.

---

## Disagreement 11 — 51:10, "Father of my lord" — who is addressed?

**EMET:** "I called upon the Lord, the father of my lord"
**LOGOS:** "I called upon the Lord, Father of my lord"
**PNEUMA:** "I called on the Lord, Father of my lord"
**Issue:** Greek Kyrie pater kyriou mou = Lord, Father of my lord. The unusual phrase may be a liturgical address, or it may mean "LORD, Father, my Lord." The capitalization affects the meaning. All agents agree on the translation; capitalization differs.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "the Lord, Father of my lord" — lowercase "lord" preserves the human referent without over-interpreting.

---

## Disagreement 12 — 51:11, "will sing praises with thanksgiving" vs. "give thanks with song"

**EMET:** "will sing praises with thanksgiving"
**LOGOS:** "give thanks with song"
**PNEUMA:** "singing songs of thanksgiving"
**Issue:** Greek kai en humnō exomologēsomai = and in a hymn I will give thanks. "Sing praises with thanksgiving" (EMET) is more literal; "give thanks with song" (LOGOS) inverts the emphasis.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "will sing praises with thanksgiving" (EMET).

---

## Disagreement 13 — 51:13, "before I went on my travels" vs. "before I had traveled far"

**EMET:** "before I went on my travels"
**LOGOS:** "before I had traveled far"
**PNEUMA:** "before I had wandered anywhere"
**Issue:** Greek prin ē planēthēnai = before wandering/traveling. EMET is most literal; LOGOS implies he did travel but was young; PNEUMA "wandered" has a negative connotation.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "before I went on my travels" (EMET).

---

## Disagreement 14 — 51:14, "before the temple I asked for her" vs. "before the temple I prayed for her"

**EMET:** "Before the temple I asked for her"
**LOGOS:** "Before the temple I prayed for her"
**PNEUMA:** "At the threshold of the temple I prayed for her"
**Issue:** Greek kata hieron prosēuxamēn peri autēs = before/near the temple I prayed for her. "Asked" (EMET) is literal for the verb; "prayed" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) is more appropriate in the liturgical context.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "Before the temple I prayed for her" (LOGOS).

---

## Disagreement 15 — 51:15, "tracked her" vs. "been on her track" vs. "been in her tracks"

**EMET:** "from my youth I have tracked her"
**LOGOS:** "from youth I have been in her tracks"
**PNEUMA:** "I have been on her trail since my youth"
**Issue:** Greek ichneuon autēn = tracking her, following her footprints. "Tracked her" (EMET) is active; "been in her tracks" (LOGOS) is passive. The active sense (Ben Sira as tracker) is more accurate.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "from my youth I have been on her track" — active but natural.

---

## Disagreement 16 — 51:19, "wrestled for her" vs. "strove toward her"

**EMET:** "My soul wrestled for her"
**LOGOS:** "My soul strove toward her"
**PNEUMA:** "My whole being wrestled for her"
**Issue:** Greek hē psychē mou eritheuthen autē = my soul was agitated/labored/wrestled for her. "Wrestled" (EMET/PNEUMA) is more vivid and apt; "strove" (LOGOS) is gentler.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "My soul wrestled toward her" — retaining "wrestled" and the directional preposition.

---

## Disagreement 17 — 51:19, "mourned my ignorance" vs. "lamented my ignorance"

**EMET:** "I mourned my ignorance of her"
**LOGOS:** "I lamented my ignorance of her"
**PNEUMA:** "I wept over how little I knew of her"
**Issue:** Greek ōdurthēn = I mourned, lamented. "Mourned" (EMET) and "lamented" (LOGOS) are both accurate. PNEUMA's "wept over" is interpretive.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "I mourned my ignorance of her" (EMET).

---

## Disagreement 18 — 51:23, "the house of instruction" — critical phrase

**EMET:** "lodge in the house of instruction"
**LOGOS:** "take up lodging in the house of instruction"
**PNEUMA:** "Make your home in the house of instruction"
**Issue:** Greek paulisthēte en oikō paideias = rest/stay in the house of learning. "House of instruction" = Hebrew bet midrash (earliest known reference). "Lodge in" (EMET) vs. "take up lodging in" (LOGOS) vs. "make your home" (PNEUMA). The invitation is to a sustained stay.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "lodge in the house of instruction" — "lodge" implies both rest and learning, and EMET/LOGOS agree.

---

## Disagreement 19 — 51:25, "Buy for yourselves without money" vs. "Buy wisdom without cost"

**EMET:** "Buy for yourselves without money"
**LOGOS:** "Buy wisdom for yourselves without cost"
**PNEUMA:** "Come, buy wisdom at no cost"
**Issue:** Greek ktēsasthe paideian aneu arguriou = acquire instruction without silver. EMET is most literal; LOGOS adds "wisdom" as the object; Isaiah 55:1 echo ("buy without money").
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "Buy for yourselves without money" (EMET) — the Isaiah echo requires preserving "money" (silver) as the absent cost.

---

## Disagreement 20 — 51:26, "she is close to find" vs. "she is near to find"

**EMET:** "she is close to find"
**LOGOS:** "she is near to find"
**PNEUMA:** "She is not far to find"
**Issue:** Greek eggus gar estin = for she is near. "Near to find" (LOGOS) is most natural English; PNEUMA inverts to negative.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "she is near to find" (LOGOS).

---

## Disagreement 21 — 51:28, "acquire teaching at the cost of much silver" vs. "acquire instruction as one would purchase much silver"

**EMET:** "Acquire teaching at the cost of much silver"
**LOGOS:** "Acquire instruction as if purchasing much silver"
**PNEUMA:** "Get instruction the way you would invest in silver"
**Issue:** Greek ktēsasthe paideian polla arguriou = acquire instruction for much silver. The sense is: invest in wisdom as heavily as you would invest in silver. "At the cost of much silver" (EMET) implies wisdom costs silver (contradicting v. 25). LOGOS "as if purchasing" preserves the comparison without contradiction.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "Acquire instruction as one would purchase much silver" (LOGOS) — the simile structure resolves the apparent contradiction with v. 25.

---

*Total disagreements logged: 21*
